Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
news.summary: A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment. Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein.

news.title: Lessons from scaling teams of frontier coding agents
news.summary: In the past year, teams of coding agents have moved from interesting demos to building large-scale software projects. Sixteen Claude agents wrote a 100,000-line C compiler that can build the Linux kernel, in a project that took about 2,000 agent sessions and $20,000 in API costs [1]. Cursor ran hundreds of agents that together wrote a web browser from scratch, more than a million lines of code, in about a week [2]. Bun was ported from Zig to Rust in 11 days, with 64 Claude agents running in parallel at its peak [3]. Each of these teams produced working software, but they differ from one another in many ways at once, from the models and roles to the scope of the projects themselves. The C compiler's agents worked as peers with no orchestrator and claimed tasks through lock files.

According to the report, approximately 8 percent of SERPs were poisoned. The altered results appeared in both desktop and mobile versions of Google Search. news.title: Wikipedians Believed AI Would Come and Go. They Were Wrong

Wikipedians battened down the hatches and made confident-sounding predictions that it would break and wash over them. Large language models might even improve Wikipedia, it was said, automating more of the housekeeping—formatting, sources, citations, missing links—and so freeing up humans to do creative work. Can Wreak Havoc.” “Too often,” she wrote, “artificial intelligence is presented as an all-powerful solution to our problems, a scalable replacement for people.” The issue confronting Wikipedia, retaining human control over machines, was the same one soon being faced everywhere. Already in 2018 Google was training AI to write “Wikipedia-like articles,” and by October 2024, a Princeton University study found that about 5 percent of nearly 3,000 newly created articles on English Wikipedia in a single month (August 2024) contained a substantial amount of AI-generated content.

Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs. These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. news.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
news.summary: Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code. But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code, meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output. A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant "bottleneck" for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in "little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment" by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is "absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process"; as "the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments." Cut once, measure twice To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish, which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual "work events" (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.Read full article Comments

news.title: Shared or dedicated inference for Embed & RerankOct 09, 20267 min read
news.summary: Choosing between shared, consumption-based inference and dedicated, provisioned inference is not simply a question of which option has the lower price.For embedding and reranking workloads, the answer depends heavily on how the application uses the model. A useful way to think about the decision is:Request Profile - > Traffic Pattern - > Utilization - > Deployment ChoiceUnderstanding these factors can tell you much more than comparing headline prices. The first question is: What does a typical model request actually look like?For embedding, request profiles can vary dramatically. Think about an e-commerce search application for a moment. Before a shopper can search for anything, every product in the store has to be turned into something the search system can match against. So the application takes each product description, runs it through the embedding model, and stores the result.

news.title: AI disqualification yields new Nikon Small World in Motion winner
news.summary: Last month we covered the winner of Nikon's Small World in Motion video: Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with a rare respiratory disorder. But allegations surfaced about Xu's use of AI while making the video. Nikon launched an investigation and concluded that Xu's entry did not comply with competition rules. The new winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam with a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism (above). According to a BBC report, some researchers expressed concern that Xu's video had structural abnormalities and that cell features appeared and disappeared in a way one would not see in actual cellular biology. Others spotted what looked like AI watermarks embedded within the source files.
